primary_claim: Adding a fact-checking reward term (verifying whether named entities in the verbalizer's description actually appear in the original tokens) to Anthropic's Natural Language Autoencoder (NLA) training objective raises the fact-checking score from 0.124 to 0.417 over 800 training steps while preserving (slightly improving) reconstruction FVE, and LLM judges preferred the new-reward model's explanations 83.6% of the time versus only 54.5% preference for the original reward recipe's post-RL model over its pre-RL model.

effect.metric: fact-checking reward g and reconstruction FVE across 800 training steps with the new reward; LLM judge preference rate
effect.value: g: 0.124 to 0.417 (step 0 to 800); FVE: 0.4126 to 0.4194; LLM judge preference for new-reward model 83.6% [75.6%, 89.4%] vs 54.5% [45.2%, 63.5%] preference for post-RL over pre-RL under the original reward

contradicts_or_qualifies: confirms and quantifies Anthropic's own flagged concern that NLA explanations can contain verifiably false claims about the target model's input context, finding about 90% of the verbalizer's specific named-entity claims are unsupported by the actual input under the original reward

corroborates a LessWrong post showing an LLM with no access to the actual activation can invent a description and reconstruct about as well as the real verbalizer that did see it, i.e. reconstruction quality (FVE) alone does not prove the verbalizer is interpreting the internal vector
limitations_stated: research was conducted on only one model, Qwen 3.6-27B
the fact-checking reward only checks exact string matches
quote: By adding the fact checking reward $g$ to the original reward function, the model learns to speak truthfully, while preserving the information later used to reconstruct the activation.
